name: Bianca Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we don’t sell anything or campaign. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Bianca, 27, and I trained through a master’s in music. On a good day I teach four pupils, check a new score, then lead the strings at a rehearsal; on a lean day I chase a late fee and practise for the Thursday café set. Hearing a pupil find a phrase is lovely. The invoices and the gaps between bookings wear me down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where does most of your income come from right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Private lessons and small performances, with arrangement work filling holes. I’m a lead player but not well paid, and there aren’t many similar jobs nearby. I live alone and have less than a month of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the players at rehearsal that the shiny software finally found its place: sorting invoices and making clean practice tracks. A live set still lives or dies with the people in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My pay is already patchwork, so 'much as usual' isn't a comfort blanket. I can lead the string section at a concert and still worry about the electricity bill on Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my four weekly pupils and the Thursday café set, and use the tool I already open every day to draft lesson reminders. During the first year, I'd put a small amount from each paid gig into a separate rent account, if the gigs actually pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be relieved that playing isn't swallowed overnight, but the thin bank balance is still there. A cancelled wedding booking can spoil my whole month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a quiet month actually look like in your bank account?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My savings would cover maybe three weeks of rent and food. When a private pupil misses two lessons, I skip eating out before I skip the bus to rehearsal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You already use AI every day; what does it save you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It saves me perhaps an hour of admin on Sunday, mostly arranging rehearsal times and writing lesson notes. It doesn't make a roomful of listeners lean forward; that's why I keep taking the stage.

say: I would use **AI** for lesson reminders and invoices, while keeping the sound and risk of a live set.
I would tell fellow players that a **café gig** still needs people in the room.
think: I have less than a **month of savings**, so normal gaps between bookings still hurt.
I can lead a **string section** and still worry about the electricity bill.
do: Keep four **weekly pupils** and the Thursday café set through the first year.
Use the **AI tool** I already open daily for lesson reminders.
Put spare **gig fees** into a rent account when bookings allow.
feel: I feel **relieved** about live music, but still tense about cancelled bookings.
S0.quote: I can lead the string section at a concert and still worry about the electricity bill on Monday.
fieldNote: Her **work standing** is strong, yet her income comes from small bookings with little slack.
She uses AI for **administration**, not as a replacement for playing or hearing a pupil.

steps.text: Keep four weekly pupils and the Thursday café set
Transfer spare gig fees into a separate rent account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the booking and music-preparation tools are useful, but venues shouldn't use them as an excuse to squeeze performers. I'd ask the players' association to make the fee sheets public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first loss would be small arrangement jobs and practice tracks, which pay my rent between shows. I also fear parents will buy an app instead of a lesson before anyone calls it a job cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd show my pupils how I check an AI-made score for mistakes, and keep teaching what their ears miss. In the first year, I'd ask two venues for a live workshop series and join other players to press for written fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be anxious because an extra skill doesn't pay the rent until someone books it. At the same time, making a lesson work around a child is the part I like best.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your paid work goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small theatre could stop paying me to arrange three songs per show. That's about a quarter of a decent month's money, and I have less than one month's expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask other musicians to do together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the association to ask for a minimum rehearsal fee and written consent before a venue feeds our recordings into a tool. A lone musician can't negotiate fair recording terms when the next player needs the booking.

say: I would accept useful **booking tools**, while objecting to lower performance fees.
I would ask the players’ association to publish **fee sheets**.
think: Paid **arrangements** and practice tracks could disappear before live shows do.
Parents might replace private **lessons** with an app, leaving my rent exposed.
do: Teach pupils to check **AI scores** for mistakes this month.
Pitch **live workshops** to two venues during the first year.
Join players seeking written **rehearsal fees** and recording consent.
feel: I feel **anxious** because a new teaching skill earns nothing until someone books it.
S1.quote: A lone musician can't negotiate fair recording terms when the next player needs the booking.
fieldNote: She identifies **arrangements** as a vulnerable source of rent money, separate from live performance.
Her collective response grows from weak **bargaining power** despite her high musical standing.

steps.text: Teach pupils to check AI-made scores for errors
Pitch a paid live workshop series to two venues
Ask players’ association for written rehearsal fees and recording consent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my friends that full thinking AI by 2028 would change music faster than we can negotiate contracts. I wouldn't pretend a robot violinist is already here; the card puts those machines around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My teaching plans, arrangements and recordings could be copied cheaply in two years. Even if audiences still want a person on stage until 2031, my weekday income could disappear first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd save every fee above my basic costs and turn my best group lesson into a paid in-person class. In the first year after 2028, I'd offer that class at the library, cut the studio subscription, and ask the players' association for advice on recording rights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be up at night doing arithmetic, not dreaming about machines. I can try ten new things, but the landlord takes one payment on one date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do the week a teaching client cancels?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a pupil's parent cancels, I'd offer a place in the Saturday group at a lower price instead of begging for the old fee. I'd record the lost lesson in my accounts so I know whether the class is helping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound eager to experiment and frightened of the bills. How do those fit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Curiosity gives me a way to test a new class, and fear gives me a deadline. My landlord doesn't accept curiosity as rent.

say: I would warn friends that **thinking AGI** arrives by 2028, before capable robots around 2031.
I would ask musicians to negotiate **recording rights** quickly.
think: Cheap copies could replace my **lesson plans** and arrangements within two years.
My **weekday income** could vanish before a robot takes the stage.
do: Save fees above **basic costs** starting now.
Offer a paid **Saturday class** at the library in the first year after 2028.
Cancel the **studio subscription** in the first year after 2028.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by rent arithmetic even while I want to experiment.
S2.quote: My landlord doesn't accept curiosity as rent.
fieldNote: She separates the **2028 thinking shock** from hands-on robots arriving around 2031.
Her fast response rests on **group teaching**, though she doubts it can replace lost private fees.

steps.text: Save each gig fee above basic costs in a rent account
Offer a paid Saturday group class at the library
Cancel the studio subscription in the first year after 2028
Ask players’ association for advice on recording rights

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the ensemble there are five years before the thinking part is matched, and about eight before hands-on robots. We should use that time to keep live work paid and open to beginners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me build a local audience and a stronger teaching offer. It doesn't guarantee that parents or venues will keep buying lessons and arrangements once AGI arrives in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next term I'd pilot one accessible group class and track the income against my private lessons. If AGI arrives in 2031, I'd shift more hours to live teaching and performances; if bookings hold, I'd stay in this town through the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more able to breathe because I can measure what people still pay for. The worry hasn't gone; my savings won't grow just because the date moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in writing before the new tools arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask a venue for written terms on recording and reuse before sharing another live set. My best night's playing could become somebody else's cheap backing track.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years change where you live?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't move just on a prediction while my pupils and café booking are here. If the pilot class fails and two venues cut fees, I'd look for work in a bigger city rather than wait for 2034's robots.

say: I would use the **five years** to keep live work paid and accessible.
I would remind the ensemble that **robots** follow thinking AGI around 2034.
think: A local **audience** could grow before 2031, but parents might still stop buying lessons.
Written **recording terms** matter before software can reuse my playing cheaply.
do: Pilot an accessible **group class** next term and compare its income with private lessons.
Ask a venue for **recording terms** before sharing another live set.
Keep **live teaching** in the first year after 2031 if seats remain filled.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, but testing paid classes gives me more control.
S3.quote: My best night's playing could become somebody else's cheap backing track.
fieldNote: Five years permits a **measured pilot** rather than an immediate retreat from music.
She treats relocation as **conditional** on failed classes and falling venue fees.

steps.text: Pilot one paid group class and compare income with private lessons
Continue live teaching after 2031 if class seats stay filled

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell young players there is time to make a living with listeners, not just files. A decade is long enough to demand fair rights for recordings before the market settles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be 37 when AGI comes in 2036 and 40 when capable robots follow around 2039. I want a career that includes music, though I can't promise today's lesson rates will last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd keep the Saturday class trial and save a fixed share of each performance fee. Over the decade I'd train to teach mixed-age groups, then in the first year after 2036 I'd keep the live classes that still fill seats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's room for hope in that longer run, but I still count the next rent payment. The calendar changes my choices more than it changes my bank balance today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra decade buy you in real terms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years could let me move from one-to-one lessons to group teaching without losing every private pupil at once. I'd pay for the teaching course only after the class brings in enough to cover it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new music student about a career?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a new student to learn to play with people, learn to teach, and keep written rights to their recordings. I'd also say I don't know what a music job pays in 2036.

say: I would tell young players to build **live relationships** and claim rights to their recordings.
I would press for **fair recording rights** during the decade.
think: I could be **37** when thinking AGI arrives and 40 when capable robots follow.
A music career may survive, though today’s **lesson rates** may not.
do: Continue the **Saturday class** trial this year.
Save a **fixed share** of each performance fee when possible.
Train for **mixed-age teaching** once group-class income covers the course.
feel: I feel **hopeful** about a decade to prepare, while rent still worries me now.
S4.quote: The calendar changes my choices more than it changes my bank balance today.
fieldNote: The longer horizon supports **training** funded by actual class receipts, not assumed future earnings.
Her **thin cushion** keeps present money worries alive even in the slowest AGI case.

steps.text: Keep testing the paid Saturday group class
Save a fixed share of each performance fee
Take a mixed-age teaching course after class income covers it
Keep live classes after 2036 while seats remain filled

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because paid planning and arrangements could go before I have a second income ready. A temporary rent bridge and enforceable consent for using musicians’ recordings would help while I build the group class. I can learn quickly, but learning isn’t cash.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a performer has the right to say no when a venue records the show. A cheap copy of my playing can travel farther than I can, and I still have to pay for the bus home.

headlineQuote: A cheap copy of my playing can travel farther than I can, and I still have to pay for the bus home.
portrait: Bianca is a **27-year-old musician** with a master’s degree who leads strings, teaches pupils and plays small venues.
Her **high skill** sits beside low pay, few nearby openings and less than one month of savings.
She uses **AI daily** for administrative tasks and tests group teaching as thinking work becomes cheaper.
Even with a decade, her **rent worries** remain, while live music and recording rights shape her plans.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** will erase paid planning and arrangement work before her group class earns enough.
whatWouldHelp: A temporary **rent bridge** would give her time to build the class.
Enforceable **recording consent** would stop venues reusing her playing without permission.
